summary: Pupils (Year 6, ages 10–11) generate and describe linear (arithmetic) number sequences, stating the term-to-term rule precisely as a signed amount and giving it with the starting number so the sequence can be rebuilt ('start at 2.5, add 1.5'; 'start at 5, subtract 2'), not a vague 'goes up/down'. The work widens to decimal and fractional steps and to decreasing sequences that stride past zero into negative numbers. A decreasing sequence is treated as 'adding a negative each time' — the same single structure as an increasing one — laying the concrete foundation for the KS3 position-to-term (nth-term) rule.
misconceptions: States the rule vaguely ('it goes down') without the amount, or gives the amount but not the starting number
Treats a decreasing sequence as a different phenomenon rather than as adding a negative each time; notices only increasing sequences
Believes the sequence 'stops' at zero — doubts that negative numbers exist or that you can go below zero
Reads or writes a negative term wrongly, e.g. −1 written or read as 1 (the raised minus sign not recognised)
Fixates on the last term and imposes a familiar pattern (4, 7, 10, 13, 16 → 18 as 'even numbers') instead of the constant step

activities.title: Number-line step machine: lay equal hops that stride past zero
steps: On a horizontal number line with zero in the MIDDLE (positives to the right, negatives to the left), set a starting number and a signed step.
Lay each term as an equal-sized hop along the line, one tap/hop at a time: e.g. start 5, step −2, so 5 → 3 → 1.
At the next hop, watch the marker stride the SAME distance straight past zero to −1, then −3, −5, −7 — the step never changed, so the sequence simply continues.
Commit to a rule in a 'state the rule' box in the form 'start at ___, add/subtract ___ each time'; if you type only 'goes down', answer the prompt 'by how much, and from where?'.
Repeat with a decimal preset (start 2.5, add 1.5) and confirm the identical equal hop works for tenths: 2.5, 4.0, 5.5, 7.0, 8.5, 10.0.
Take a 'predict the 10th term' challenge that rewards using the rule/structure rather than counting on one by one.
activities.insight: A linear sequence has one constant signed step; because the step never changes at zero, the sequence does not stop or bounce — it continues into the negatives. A rule that names BOTH a start and a signed amount uniquely rebuilds the whole sequence, and the same structure covers increasing, decreasing, whole-number and decimal cases.

activities.title: State a rule precise enough to rebuild the sequence
steps: Continue 5, 3, 1, … and give the next four numbers (−1, −3, −5, −7), then state the rule as 'start at 5, subtract 2 each time'.
Continue 2.5, 4.0, 5.5, … and give the next three numbers (7.0, 8.5, 10.0), then state the rule as 'start at 2.5, add 1.5 each time'.
Phrase each rule so clearly that a partner could rebuild the whole sequence from the words alone, without seeing the numbers.
Test your own rule: use only your stated start and signed amount to regenerate the given terms and check they match.
activities.insight: The term-to-term rule gives the exact signed step; together with the starting number, it pins down the sequence so anyone can reconstruct it from the words alone.

activities.title: Check every step, not just the last term
steps: Consider 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 continued by someone as 18 'because they look even-ish'. Decide what the next term should be and explain why.
Find the step between EVERY adjacent pair, not just the last two, to confirm the constant step (+3) and the correct next term (19).
Explain to the person why fixating on the surface feature of the last number (its being even/odd) is not the rule.
Decide whether a wrong term is a slip (a miscount) or a misconception (a misread rule) by re-checking the step between each pair.
activities.insight: A linear sequence is defined by the same step between every pair of terms; the next term follows the step, not a surface pattern noticed in the last number alone.

activities.title: Negative terms in real below-zero contexts
steps: Read and write negative terms on a temperature scale or a number track that extends below zero (sea level, floors below ground).

Point to −1 versus 1 and say the difference aloud, noting that the minus sign in front of the number marks it as negative (some resources raise this sign to distinguish it from the subtraction operation).
Continue a sequence that crosses zero in context (e.g. temperatures 3, 1, −1, −3, …) and read each term correctly.
Calculate the interval across zero (e.g. from 1 to −3) by counting the equal steps along the line.
activities.insight: Negative numbers are real positions to the left of zero; a decreasing sequence reaches and passes them by the same equal step, and the sign must be read and written to tell −1 apart from 1.

checkQuestion: Carry each of these on and tell me the rule you are using. First: 5, 3, 1, … give me the next four numbers. Then: 2.5, 4.0, 5.5, … give me the next three. Tell me each rule so clearly that I could rebuild the whole sequence from your words alone.
checkAnswer: First: −1, −3, −5, −7; rule 'start at 5, subtract 2 each time' (the equal step of −2 continues past zero into the negatives). Second: 7.0, 8.5, 10.0; rule 'start at 2.5, add 1.5 each time'.
